newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's Mahathir maintains grip on party.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's Mahathir maintains grip on party.

text.p: Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad showed he is still very much in charge at the end of his party's political convention at which he railed about "money politics", analysts said at the weekend.

Political analysts said the triennial elections of the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) were basically a victory for Mahathir, a medical doctor who took over leadership of the party and country in 1981.
The elections, which drew nearly 1,900 UMNO delegates, are generally viewed as more significant than general polls.
But Mahathir, who was uncontested in his post as UMNO president this year, brushed aside questions about whether he would stand for re-election in the 1999 party polls.
"Why should we look so far ahead?" he said in response to reporters' questions on Saturday.
The 70-year-old Mahathir has said he and Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, who is UMNO vice president, are willing to contest their posts if the fight is clean.

Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi, a staunch Mahathir man, won one of the three vice presidencies and other loyalists snared most of the positions on the policy-making Supreme Advisory Council in the elections this week.
Youth and Sports Minister Muhyiddin Yassin, who won the most number of votes in the 1993 polls as a member of Anwar's "vision team", came in next to last in a seven-man field this time.
"We have seen another masterful performance from Dr Mahathir," said University of Malaya economics professor Murugesu Pathmanathan. "It shows he's still very much in control of his party."

The UMNO-dominated National Front coalition has governed Malaysia since independence in 1957, always winning elections handily. By political convention, UMNO's president and deputy president become prime minister and deputy and past party conventions have seen keen tussles for these posts.

But alarmed at the growing trend towards vote-buying and other abuses lumped under the name "money politics", the UMNO leadership agreed there would be no contest for the top two posts and a blanket ban on campaigning for all other offices.
Analysts viewed the elections as a kind of proxy battle between Mahathir and his 49-year-old deputy, who many think is destined to succeed the prime minister at the next convention.

But the first round of polls looked like a setback for Mahathir after two of his allies, Trade and Industry Minister Rafidah Aziz and Rahim Tamby Chik, lost the chairmanships of the women's and youth's wings of the party.
Then came the most dramatic moment of the four-day convention, when Mahathir appeared to break down in sobs after an emotional denunciation of corruption in the party.
Delegates, some in tears themselves, leapt to their feet in a standing ovation, shouting: "Long live Mahathir", leaving cynics wondering at the depths of the prime minister's angst.
Mahathir, in any case, denied he had become emotional. "I thought I was speaking normally," he told reporters afterward.
Whatever the impact of Mahathir's words or tears, all the corporate figures in the polls held just after the speech lost their races and many of Anwar's people were defeated as well.

In his speech, Mahathir raised the question of who was providing the huge sums of money that it now takes to mount a campaign in UMNO. "Perhaps rich supporters helped. But is this money free? Is this not corruption?" he asked.
The 1993 UMNO election convention, which propelled Anwar into the deputy leadership position, also saw for the first time strong representation by corporate and professional figures.
UMNO has traditionally been a party dominated by teachers and civil servants.

Asked if corporations were a major corrupting influence on UMNO, Mahthir told reporters on Friday: "There are indications of course, but I do not like to presume anything until I have the correct information."
Mahathir's campaign against money politics coincided with the return of dissident UMNO members on the eve of the party convention.
The dissident Spirit of 46 party was formed after Mahathir's arch political rival, Tengku Razaleigh Hamzah, mounted an unsuccessful challenge against him in the 1987 campaign.
